claim: Soybean oil (SBO) consumption in the United States increased dramatically over the past century.
source: Over the past century, soybean oil (SBO) consumption in the United States increased dramatically.
evidence: This is a factual statement about historical dietary trends in the United States.

claim: Linoleic acid (18:2) is the main fatty acid in soybean oil.
source: The main SBO fatty acid, linoleic acid (18:2), inhibits in vitro the growth of lactobacilli, beneficial members of the small intestinal microbiota.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about the composition of soybean oil.

claim: Linoleic acid (18:2) inhibits in vitro the growth of lactobacilli.
source: The main SBO fatty acid, linoleic acid (18:2), inhibits in vitro the growth of lactobacilli, beneficial members of the small intestinal microbiota.
evidence: This is a statement about experimental observations of 18:2 effects on lactobacilli in vitro.

claim: Lactobacilli are beneficial members of the small intestinal microbiota.
source: The main SBO fatty acid, linoleic acid (18:2), inhibits in vitro the growth of lactobacilli, beneficial members of the small intestinal microbiota.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the role of lactobacilli.

claim: Human-associated lactobacilli have declined in prevalence in Western microbiomes.
source: Human-associated lactobacilli have declined in prevalence in Western microbiomes, but how dietary changes may have impacted their ecology is unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about observed trends in Western microbiomes.

claim: Directed evolution in vitro in L. reuteri and L. johnsonii led to strong 18:2 resistance with mutations in genes for lipid biosynthesis, acid stress, and the cell membrane or wall.
source: Directed evolution in vitro in both species led to strong 18:2 resistance with mutations in genes for lipid biosynthesis, acid stress, and the cell membrane or wall.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the in vitro evolution experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Small-intestinal Lactobacillus populations in mice were unaffected by chronic and acute 18:2 exposure.
source: Small-intestinal Lactobacillus populations in mice were unaffected by chronic and acute 18:2 exposure, yet harbored both 18:2- sensitive and resistant strains.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mouse experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Small-intestinal Lactobacillus populations in mice harbored both 18:2-sensitive and resistant strains.
source: Small-intestinal Lactobacillus populations in mice were unaffected by chronic and acute 18:2 exposure, yet harbored both 18:2- sensitive and resistant strains.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the isolation and testing of lactobacilli strains from mice.

claim: Extant small intestinal lactobacilli are protected from toxic dietary components via the gut environment.
source: This work shows that extant small intestinal lactobacilli are protected from toxic dietary components via the gut environment as well as their own capacity to evolve resistance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations in the manuscript.

claim: Extant small intestinal lactobacilli are protected from toxic dietary components via their own capacity to evolve resistance.
source: This work shows that extant small intestinal lactobacilli are protected from toxic dietary components via the gut environment as well as their own capacity to evolve resistance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro evolution experiments.

claim: Antibiotics can cause lasting alterations to the microbiome.
source: While antibiotics can cause lasting alterations to the microbiome (David et al., 2014a; Dethlefsen et al., 2008; Dethlefsen and Relman, 2011; Jakobsson et al., 2010), dietary perturbations rarely do so (Sonnenburg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Dietary perturbations rarely cause lasting alterations to the microbiome.
source: While antibiotics can cause lasting alterations to the microbiome (David et al., 2014a; Dethlefsen et al., 2008; Dethlefsen and Relman, 2011; Jakobsson et al., 2010), dietary perturbations rarely do so (Sonnenburg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The gut microbiome can be quickly altered by diet but community composition generally recovers within days in humans and mice.
source: In humans and in mice, the gut microbiome can be quickly altered by diet but community composition generally recovers within days (Carmody et al., 2015; David et al., 2014a; David et al., 2014b; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Resilience to dietary perturbation may be direct, as gut microbes functionally adapt to diet.
source: Resilience to dietary perturbation may be direct, as gut microbes functionally adapt to diet, or indirect through buffering by the gut habitat.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about mechanisms of microbiome resilience.

claim: Resilience to dietary perturbation may be indirect through buffering by the gut habitat.
source: Resilience to dietary perturbation may be direct, as gut microbes functionally adapt to diet, or indirect through buffering by the gut habitat.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about mechanisms of microbiome resilience.

claim: Soybean oil consumption in the United States increased from less than 0.001 kg/person/year to 12 kg/person/year during the 20th century.
source: During the 20th century, the greatest dietary change in the United States was in the consumption of soybean oil (SBO), which increased from less than 0.001 kg/person/year to 12 kg/person/year (Blasbalg et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative claim supported by a citation.

claim: The increase in soybean oil consumption was the greatest dietary change in the United States during the 20th century.
source: During the 20th century, the greatest dietary change in the United States was in the consumption of soybean oil (SBO), which increased from less than 0.001 kg/person/year to 12 kg/person/year (Blasbalg et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Conventional soybean oil is a mixture of triglycerides composed of five long chain fatty acids.
source: Conventional ('commodity') soybean oil, frequently labeled as 'vegetable oil', is a mixture of triglycerides composed of five long chain fatty acids (FAs), with linoleic acid (18:2) comprising over 50% of the FAs.
evidence: This is a statement about the chemical composition of soybean oil.

claim: Linoleic acid (18:2) comprises over 50% of the fatty acids in conventional soybean oil.
source: Conventional ('commodity') soybean oil, frequently labeled as 'vegetable oil', is a mixture of triglycerides composed of five long chain fatty acids (FAs), with linoleic acid (18:2) comprising over 50% of the FAs.
evidence: This is a statement about the chemical composition of soybean oil.

claim: Triglycerides are hydrolyzed by lipases active in the saliva, stomach, and upper duodenum.
source: After triglycerides are hydrolyzed by lipases active in the saliva, stomach, and upper duodenum, free FAs and monoglycerides are absorbed in the small intestine (Mansbach et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Free fatty acids and monoglycerides are absorbed in the small intestine.
source: After triglycerides are hydrolyzed by lipases active in the saliva, stomach, and upper duodenum, free FAs and monoglycerides are absorbed in the small intestine (Mansbach et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The microbiota of the human small intestine is exposed to fatty acids during the absorption process.
source: The microbiota of the human small intestine is exposed to FAs during this process (El Aidy et al., 2015; Kishino et al., 2013): therefore, an increase in the concentration of specific FAs has the potential to reshape microbial communities and select for microbes that thrive in the novel environment.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: An increase in the concentration of specific fatty acids has the potential to reshape microbial communities and select for microbes that thrive in the novel environment.
source: The microbiota of the human small intestine is exposed to FAs during this process (El Aidy et al., 2015; Kishino et al., 2013): therefore, an increase in the concentration of specific FAs has the potential to reshape microbial communities and select for microbes that thrive in the novel environment.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the exposure of microbiota to fatty acids.

claim: Linoleic acid, oleic acid, and alpha-linolenic acid are known to be bacteriostatic and/or bactericidal to small intestinal bacteria as non-esterified fatty acids in vitro at concentrations found in the small intestine.
source: Linoleic acid and the other two major unsaturated FAs in SBO, oleic acid (18:1), and alpha-linolenic acid (18:3), are known to be bacteriostatic and/or bactericidal to small intestinal bacteria as non-esterified (free) fatty acids in vitro at concentrations found in the small intestine (Kabara et al., 1972; Kankaanpää et al., 2001; Kodicek, 1945; Nieman, 1954).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The primary modes of killing by unsaturated fatty acids include permeabilization of cell membranes.
source: The primary modes of killing include permeabilization of cell membranes (Greenway and Dyke, 1979) and interference with FA metabolism (Zheng et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The primary modes of killing by unsaturated fatty acids include interference with fatty acid metabolism.
source: The primary modes of killing include permeabilization of cell membranes (Greenway and Dyke, 1979) and interference with FA metabolism (Zheng et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Affected microbes by unsaturated fatty acids are predominantly Gram-positive bacteria including the genus Lactobacillus.
source: Affected microbes are predominantly Gram-positive bacteria including the genus Lactobacillus (Nieman, 1954).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Lactobacilli are considered beneficial members of the human small intestine.
source: Lactobacilli are particularly important as they are considered beneficial members of the human small intestine (Walsh et al., 2008; Walter et al., 2007; Walter et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Lactobacilli have been shown to be growth inhibited by the specific fatty acids present in soybean oil.
source: They have been shown to be growth inhibited by the specific FAs present in SBO (Boyaval et al., 1995; De Weirdt et al., 2013; Jenkins and Courtney, 2003; Jiang et al., 1998; Kabara et al., 1972; Kankaanpää et al., 2001; Kodicek, 1945; Raychowdhury et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The human-associated L. reuteri underwent a population bottleneck that coincides with the increase in soybean oil consumption in the U.S.
source: It is interesting to note that the human-associated L. reuteri underwent a population bottleneck that coincides with the increase in SBO consumption in the U.S. and is far less prevalent than it was in the past (Walter et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: L. reuteri is far less prevalent in humans than it was in the past.
source: It is interesting to note that the human-associated L. reuteri underwent a population bottleneck that coincides with the increase in SBO consumption in the U.S. and is far less prevalent than it was in the past (Walter et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: L. reuteri and other lactobacilli persist in the small intestine of Western individuals, suggesting mechanisms to counter the inhibitory effects of fatty acids in vivo.
source: Despite its decline, L. reuteri and other lactobacilli persist in the small intestine of Western individuals, suggesting mechanisms to counter the inhibitory effects of FAs in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that lactobacilli persist despite fatty acid exposure.

claim: L. reuteri ATCC 53608 growth is inhibited by free 18:1, 18:2, and 18:3 in disc diffusion assays.
source: We observed growth inhibition of this strain by free 18:1, 18:2, and 18:3 (Figure 1A), and this inhibition occurred in the presence of completely hydrolyzed SBO (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The inhibition of L. reuteri ATCC 53608 by unsaturated fatty acids occurred in the presence of completely hydrolyzed soybean oil.
source: We observed growth inhibition of this strain by free 18:1, 18:2, and 18:3 (Figure 1A), and this inhibition occurred in the presence of completely hydrolyzed SBO (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The two saturated free fatty acids 16:0 and 18:0 and glycerol did not interfere with L. reuteri ATCC 53608 growth.
source: The two saturated free FAs 16:0 and 18:0 and glycerol did not interfere with growth.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from disc diffusion assays.

claim: 18:2 permeabilized L. reuteri ATCC 53608 cells with an estimated IC50 of 20 μg/ml (p < 0.001).
source: We observed that 18:2 permeabilized the cells with an estimated inhibitory concentration 50 (IC50) of 20 μg/ml (p < 0.001) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from a cell permeability assay shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The IC50 of 18:2 for L. reuteri ATCC 53608 concurs with estimates of the concentration of 18:2 present in a mouse consuming a soybean oil diet (11 to 28 μg/ml for a mouse on a 7% by weight SBO diet).
source: This IC50 concurs with our estimates of the concentration of 18:2 present in a mouse consuming a SBO diet (11 to 28 μg/ml for a mouse on a 7% by weight SBO diet, see Materials and methods) and with previous estimates of mammalian physiological relevant concentrations of unsaturated FAs (Kankaanpää et al., 2001; Kodicek, 1945).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data with calculated estimates and previous literature.

claim: The IC50 of 18:2 for L. reuteri ATCC 53608 concurs with previous estimates of mammalian physiological relevant concentrations of unsaturated fatty acids.
source: This IC50 concurs with our estimates of the concentration of 18:2 present in a mouse consuming a SBO diet (11 to 28 μg/ml for a mouse on a 7% by weight SBO diet, see Materials and methods) and with previous estimates of mammalian physiological relevant concentrations of unsaturated FAs (Kankaanpää et al., 2001; Kodicek, 1945).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Physiological levels of 18:2 were toxic to L. reuteri in vitro.
source: Thus, physiological levels of 18:2 were toxic to L. reuteri in vitro.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the IC50 measurement and comparison to physiological concentrations.

claim: The basal, rodent-associated L. reuteri strains on average were inhibited by 18:2 more strongly than the other strains (Kruskal-Wallis test, p < 10−4).
source: We observed that the basal, rodent-associated strains on average were inhibited by 18:2 more strongly than the other strains (Kruskal-Wallis test, p < 10−4) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from testing 40 L. reuteri strains, shown in Figure 2.

claim: Considerable variation in 18:2 resistance was observed within host sources of L. reuteri strains.
source: However, we observed considerable variation within host sources, and the human-associated strains were no more resistant to 18:2 than the strains derived from pig, poultry, or sourdough.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from testing 40 L. reuteri strains.

claim: Human-associated L. reuteri strains were no more resistant to 18:2 than the strains derived from pig, poultry, or sourdough.
source: However, we observed considerable variation within host sources, and the human-associated strains were no more resistant to 18:2 than the strains derived from pig, poultry, or sourdough.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from testing 40 L. reuteri strains.

claim: Within human L. reuteri strains, 18:2 resistance did not relate to L. reuteri isolation site.
source: Moreover, within human strains, 18:2 resistance did not relate to L. reuteri isolation site (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There did not appear to be a clear relationship of 18:2 resistance with L. reuteri clades as defined by Oh et al., 2010.
source: There also did not appear to be a clear relationship of 18:2 resistance with L. reuteri clades as defined by Oh et al., 2010 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: All of the evolved lactobacilli populations showed smaller zones of inhibition around 18:2 and 18:3 in a disc diffusion assay compared to their respective starting strains.
source: At the end of the passaging regime, all of the evolved lactobacilli populations showed smaller zones of inhibition around 18:2 and 18:3 in a disc diffusion assay compared to their respective starting strains (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the in vitro evolution experiment, shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Isolates LR2-1 and LJ41072 showed 18:2 resistance in liquid culture supplemented with 18:2.
source: We tested isolates LR2-1 from population LR2 and LJ41072 from population LJ4 in liquid culture supplemented with 18:2 to confirm their 18:2 resistance (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: 30 mutational events in 15 genes were observed across the five L. reuteri populations.
source: After requiring mutations have a minimum frequency of 10% in a population and confirming all mutations were not due to potential mismapping, we observed 30 mutational events in 15 genes across the five L. reuteri populations and 35 mutational events in 21 genes in the four L. johnsonii populations.
evidence: This is a primary finding from whole genome sequencing of evolved populations.

claim: 35 mutational events in 21 genes were observed in the four L. johnsonii populations.
source: After requiring mutations have a minimum frequency of 10% in a population and confirming all mutations were not due to potential mismapping, we observed 30 mutational events in 15 genes across the five L. reuteri populations and 35 mutational events in 21 genes in the four L. johnsonii populations.
evidence: This is a primary finding from whole genome sequencing of evolved populations.

claim: In each L. reuteri and L. johnsonii population, a few mutations had swept the entire population.
source: In each population, a few mutations had swept the entire population (Tables 1 and 2, Supplementary file 3 and 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding from whole genome sequencing of evolved populations.

claim: Both the L. reuteri and L. johnsonii populations bore high frequency variants (>60%) in genes relating to fatty acid metabolism, ion transport, and the cell membrane/wall.
source: Both the L. reuteri and L. johnsonii populations bore high frequency variants (>60%) in genes relating to FA metabolism, ion transport, and the cell membrane/wall.
evidence: This is a primary finding from whole genome sequencing of evolved populations.

claim: The LR2 18 bp deletion in FabT was able to enhance 18:2 resistance in L. reuteri 6475.
source: The LR2 18 bp deletion and the LR5 SNP in FabT present alone were able to enhance 18:2 resistance in L. reuteri 6475, similar to that observed for the total LR2 and LR5 populations (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from recombineering experiments, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The LR5 SNP in FabT was able to enhance 18:2 resistance in L. reuteri 6475.
source: The LR2 18 bp deletion and the LR5 SNP in FabT present alone were able to enhance 18:2 resistance in L. reuteri 6475, similar to that observed for the total LR2 and LR5 populations (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from recombineering experiments, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The LR5 SNP in the hydrolase gene was not sufficient to render the strain observably 18:2 resistant by a disc diffusion assay.
source: The LR5 SNP in the hydrolase gene, however, was not sufficient to render the strain observably 18:2 resistant by a disc diffusion assay.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from recombineering experiments.

claim: Mice on the HF diet gained significantly more fat mass than mice on the LF diet (p = 1.53*10−4).
source: While the mice on the HF diet gained significantly more fat mass (p = 1.53*10−4, mean in HF diet group = 0.043, mean in LF diet group = 0.028, 95% CI = (0.0076, 0.0218), two-sample, two-tailed t-test on epididymal fat pad mass), we observed no differences between the total microbiome composition of the jejuna of mice on the two diets (PERMANOVA on the total cell population, p > 0.5).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the mouse diet experiment.

claim: No differences were observed between the total microbiome composition of the jejuna of mice on the LF and HF diets (PERMANOVA on the total cell population, p > 0.5).
source: While the mice on the HF diet gained significantly more fat mass (p = 1.53*10−4, mean in HF diet group = 0.043, mean in LF diet group = 0.028, 95% CI = (0.0076, 0.0218), two-sample, two-tailed t-test on epididymal fat pad mass), we observed no differences between the total microbiome composition of the jejuna of mice on the two diets (PERMANOVA on the total cell population, p > 0.5).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from 16S rRNA gene sequencing of mouse jejunal contents.

claim: OTU 363731 mapping to Akkermansia muciniphila was 60-fold enriched in the HF diet (Kruskal-Wallis test, FDR < 0.1).
source: Using a Kruskal-Wallis test, with FDR < 0.1, we observed that OTU 363731 mapping to Akkermansia muciniphila was 60-fold enriched in the HF diet.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from 16S rRNA gene sequencing of mouse jejunal contents.

claim: The level of soybean oil and compensatory reduction in carbohydrates in the HF diet was not sufficient to greatly alter the microbiome.
source: These results imply that the level of SBO and compensatory reduction in carbohydrates in the HF diet was not sufficient to greatly alter the microbiome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that the microbiome composition was similar between diets.

claim: OTUs 692154 and 592160, taxonomically assigned to L. reuteri and L. johnsonii, respectively, were the two most abundant lactobacilli OTUs in all samples.
source: OTUs 692154 and 592160, taxonomically assigned by Greengenes to L. reuteri and L. johnsonii, respectively, were the two most abundant lactobacilli OTUs in all samples.
evidence: This is a primary finding from 16S rRNA gene sequencing of mouse jejunal contents.

claim: L. reuteri OTU 692154 and L. johnsonii OTU 592160 displayed comparable relative abundances in the LF and HF diets (total aliquot; Kruskal-Wallis test and ANOVA on a linear mixed model to include cage effects, p values > 0.05).
source: These OTUs displayed comparable relative abundances in the two diets (total aliquot; Kruskal-Wallis test and ANOVA on a linear mixed model to include cage effects, p values > 0.05, Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from 16S rRNA gene sequencing, shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: L. reuteri OTU 692154 and L. johnsonii OTU 592160 were present in the 18:2, live-only microbiota in both sets of mice.
source: These L. reuteri and L. johnsonii OTUs were present in the 18:2, live-only microbiota in both sets of mice (Figure 4C and D), suggesting these taxa survived the 18:2 acute treatment regardless of the dietary fat content.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from 16S rRNA gene sequencing, shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: L. reuteri OTU 692154 and L. johnsonii OTU 592160 survived the 18:2 acute treatment regardless of the dietary fat content.
source: These L. reuteri and L. johnsonii OTUs were present in the 18:2, live-only microbiota in both sets of mice (Figure 4C and D), suggesting these taxa survived the 18:2 acute treatment regardless of the dietary fat content.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of these OTUs in the live-only microbiota after 18:2 gavage.

claim: L. reuteri OTU 692154 was detected at very low levels in the microbiota of mice housed in three out of six LF diet cages and in two out of six HF diet cages.
source: Note we detected L. reuteri OTU 692154 at very low levels in the microbiota of mice housed in three out of six LF diet cages and in two out of six HF diet cages (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from 16S rRNA gene sequencing, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: L. johnsonii OTU 592160 enriched 2- to 5-fold in the live-only microbiota after 18:2 gavage (ANOVA on a linear mixed model to include cage effects and Kruskal-Wallis tests, p values < 0.01).
source: Comparison of the relative abundance of these two OTUs in the total and live-only microbiota revealed these lactobacilli (with the exception of L. reuteri in the LF diet) enriched 2- to 5-fold (ANOVA on a linear mixed model to include cage effects and Kruskal-Wallis tests, p values < 0.01) after 18:2 gavage.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from 16S rRNA gene sequencing.

claim: The live-only microbiota of HF diet mice had an enrichment of 11 lactobacilli OTUs after 18:2 gavage (5- to 9-fold enrichment compared to control gavage, Kruskal-Wallis, FDRs < 0.1).
source: Furthermore, the live-only microbiota of HF diet mice had an enrichment of 11 lactobacilli OTUs after 18:2 gavage (5- to 9-fold enrichment compared to control gavage, Kruskal-Wallis, FDRs < 0.1, Figure 4—figure supplement 2D) at the expense of Allobaculum spp.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from 16S rRNA gene sequencing, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Lactobacilli enriched in the live-only microbiota of HF diet mice after 18:2 gavage at the expense of Allobaculum spp.
source: Furthermore, the live-only microbiota of HF diet mice had an enrichment of 11 lactobacilli OTUs after 18:2 gavage (5- to 9-fold enrichment compared to control gavage, Kruskal-Wallis, FDRs < 0.1, Figure 4—figure supplement 2D) at the expense of Allobaculum spp.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from 16S rRNA gene sequencing, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Lactobacilli resist acute 18:2 exposure particularly in the context of a high-18:2 diet.
source: These observations suggest that lactobacilli resist acute 18:2 exposure particularly in the context of a high-18:2 diet.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enrichment of lactobacilli in the live-only microbiota after 18:2 gavage.

claim: No difference was observed between the saline and 18:2 gavage samples for either diet in the qPCR analysis of Lactobacillus copy number (two-sample, two-tailed t-test, p values > 0.1).
source: We observed no difference between the saline and 18:2 gavage samples for either diet (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E, two-sample, two-tailed t-test, p values > 0.1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from qPCR analysis, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E.

claim: L. reuteri isolates recovered from the HF-diet fed mice were on average more resistant to 18:2 than L. reuteri isolated from the LF-diet fed mice (113 isolates from 15 mice in eight cages Kruskal-Wallis, p < 0.05).
source: While most isolates were sensitive to 18:2, we observed that L. reuteri isolates recovered from the HF-diet fed mice were on average more resistant to 18:2 than L. reuteri isolated from the LF-diet fed mice (113 isolates from 15 mice in eight cages Kruskal-Wallis, p < 0.05, Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from testing isolates in liquid culture, shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Chronic exposure to a diet high in 18:2 promotes resistance in the resident L. reuteri population.
source: This observation is consistent with the hypothesis that chronic exposure to a diet high in 18:2 promotes resistance in the resident L. reuteri population.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that HF diet isolates were more resistant to 18:2.

claim: No correlation was observed between the ability of L. reuteri strains to grow in vitro in 18:2 and their abundance in mice gavaged with 18:2 for mice on either diet.
source: We observed no correlation between the ability of these strains to grow in vitro in 18:2 and their abundance in mice gavaged with 18:2 for mice on either diet (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B and C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B and C.

claim: The mouse gut environment protects susceptible L. reuteri strains.
source: With this caveat in mind, these results indicate that while chronic exposure to 18:2 can result in L. reuteri strains with higher 18:2 resistance, the mouse gut environment protects susceptible strains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of correlation between in vitro resistance and in vivo abundance.

claim: All L. johnsonii isolates were sensitive to 18:2.
source: We partially replicated these findings with L. johnsonii: all isolates were sensitive to 18:2, but L. johnsonii from the HF diet-fed mice were more strongly inhibited by 18:2 than those isolated from the LF-fed mice (159 isolates from 22 mice in 12 cages; Kruskal-Wallis, p < 0.001, Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from testing isolates in liquid culture, shown in Figure 4E.

claim: L. johnsonii from the HF diet-fed mice were more strongly inhibited by 18:2 than those isolated from the LF-fed mice (159 isolates from 22 mice in 12 cages; Kruskal-Wallis, p < 0.001).
source: We partially replicated these findings with L. johnsonii: all isolates were sensitive to 18:2, but L. johnsonii from the HF diet-fed mice were more strongly inhibited by 18:2 than those isolated from the LF-fed mice (159 isolates from 22 mice in 12 cages; Kruskal-Wallis, p < 0.001, Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from testing isolates in liquid culture, shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The comparison of LRHF to LR0 revealed 71 mutations in 60 genes with functions predominantly in DNA metabolism, energy metabolism, and environmental response.
source: The comparison revealed 71 mutations in 60 genes with functions predominantly in DNA metabolism, energy metabolism, and environmental response (Table 3, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from whole genome sequencing of LRHF and LR0.

claim: None of the genes mutated in the in vitro evolution assay differed between LR0 and LRHF.
source: None of the genes mutated in the in vitro evolution assay differed between LR0 and LFHF.
evidence: This is a primary finding from comparing mutations in LRHF to those in the in vitro evolved strains.

claim: LRHF exhibited mutations in a sodium-hydrogen antiporter gene and a peroxide stress (PerF) gene, both of which may represent adaptation to an acidic environment caused by exposure to fatty acids.
source: LRHF exhibited mutations in a sodium-hydrogen antiporter gene and a peroxide stress (PerF) gene, both of which may represent adaptation to an acidic environment caused by exposure to FAs.
evidence: This is a primary finding from whole genome sequencing of LRHF, with speculation about the functional significance.

claim: LRHF exhibited mutations in a membrane-bound lytic murein transglycosylase D precursor involved in the production of the peptidoglycan layer.
source: Of potential relevance to FA exposure, we observed mutations in a membrane-bound lytic murein transglycosylase D precursor involved in the production of the peptidoglycan layer (Vollmer et al., 2008) and the fructosyltransferase Ftf involved in the production of exopolysaccharide (Sims et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a primary finding from whole genome sequencing of LRHF, supported by citations about gene function.

claim: LRHF exhibited mutations in the fructosyltransferase Ftf involved in the production of exopolysaccharide.
source: Of potential relevance to FA exposure, we observed mutations in a membrane-bound lytic murein transglycosylase D precursor involved in the production of the peptidoglycan layer (Vollmer et al., 2008) and the fructosyltransferase Ftf involved in the production of exopolysaccharide (Sims et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a primary finding from whole genome sequencing of LRHF, supported by citations about gene function.

claim: Exposure to 18:2 in vivo does not invoke selection on the same genes that are implicated in 18:2 resistance in vitro.
source: These results suggest that exposure to 18:2 in vivo does not invoke selection on the same genes that are implicated in 18:2 resistance in vitro.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of overlap in mutated genes between LRHF and the in vitro evolved strains.

claim: The mutations acquired by 18:2 in vitro adapted lactobacilli strains are consistent with the known bacteriostatic and bactericidal mechanisms of 18:2.
source: The mutations our 18:2 in vitro adapted lactobacilli strains acquired are consistent with the known bacteriostatic and bactericidal mechanisms of 18:2: by increasing membrane fluidity and permeability (Greenway and Dyke, 1979) potentially leading to cell lysis or leakage (Galbraith and Miller, 1973b; Parsons et al., 2012), by blocking absorption of essential nutrients (Nieman, 1954), and by inhibiting FA synthesis (Zheng et al., 2005) and oxidative phosphorylation (Galbraith and Miller, 1973a).
evidence: This is an inference based on the types of genes mutated, supported by citations about 18:2 mechanisms of action.

claim: Lactobacilli are capable of combating 18:2 toxicity by converting 18:2 to conjugated 18:2 and subsequently a monounsaturated or saturated fatty acid.
source: Lactobacilli are also capable of combating 18:2 toxicity by converting 18:2 to conjugated 18:2 and subsequently a monounsaturated or saturated fatty acid (Jenkins and Courtney, 2003; Kishino et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: No mutations were recovered in genes known to be involved in the production of conjugated 18:2.
source: We did not recover any mutations in genes known to be involved in the production of conjugated 18:2.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the whole genome sequencing of evolved strains.

claim: Mouse-associated L. reuteri and L. johnsonii were present at equivalent relative abundances in mice fed diets high or low in 18:2.
source: Despite the toxicity of 18:2 towards lactobacilli, mouse-associated L. reuteri and L. johnsonii were present at equivalent relative abundances in mice fed diets high or low in 18:2.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mouse diet experiment.

claim: L. reuteri and L. johnsonii survived a gavage of 18:2 equal to double what mice normally encounter in their daily diet.
source: Moreover, these microbes survived a gavage of 18:2 equal to double what mice normally encounter in their daily diet.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mouse gavage experiment.

claim: The results are consistent with the findings of Holmes and colleagues, who analyzed the fecal microbiomes of mice on 25 different SBO diets varying in their macronutrient composition.
source: Our results are consistent with the findings of Holmes and colleagues, who analyzed the fecal microbiomes of mice on 25 different SBO diets varying in their macronutrient (fat, protein, carbohydrate) composition.
evidence: This is a comparison to a previous study.

claim: Holmes and colleagues demonstrated that fat has only a minor effect on microbiome structure.
source: Their results demonstrate that fat has only a minor effect on microbiome structure (Holmes et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In microbial systems engineered for waste processing, concentrations of linoleic acid within the range predicted to be consumed by animals can cause failure of the desired microbial biodegradation processes.
source: In contrast, in microbial systems engineered for waste processing, concentrations of linoleic acid within the range predicted to be consumed by animals can cause failure of the desired microbial biodegradation processes (Lalman and Bagley, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The resistance of lactobacilli to linoleic acid in the mouse host is inferred to be dependent on the complexity of the gut habitat.
source: The resistance of lactobacilli to linoleic acid in the mouse host is therefore inferred to be dependent on the complexity of the gut habitat.
evidence: This is an inference based on the contrast between in vitro toxicity and in vivo survival.

claim: In mice, lactobacilli colonize both the small intestine and forestomach.
source: In mice, lactobacilli colonize both the small intestine and forestomach (Walter et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Fat digestion occurs primarily in the small intestine in mice.
source: While lingual lipases exist in mice (DeNigris et al., 1988), fat digestion occurs primarily in the small intestine.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study and general knowledge of mammalian physiology.

claim: Forestomach microbes should not be exposed to a high concentration of free fatty acids.
source: As a result, forestomach microbes should not be exposed to a high concentration of free FAs, and SBO itself is not toxic.
evidence: This is an inference based on the location of fat digestion.

claim: A gavage of 18:2 exposes forestomach microbes to free 18:2.
source: A gavage of 18:2, on the other hand, exposes forestomach microbes to free 18:2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the method of gavage delivery.

claim: Lactobacilli may be protected from direct exposure to free fatty acids by their capacity to form a dense biofilm on non-mucus secreting stratified epithelial cells.
source: Lactobacilli may be protected from this direct exposure by their capacity to form a dense biofilm on non-mucus secreting stratified epithelial cells (Frese et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In the 1960's and 1970's prior to the emergence of SBO as a major dietary fat source, L. reuteri was recovered from the intestinal tract of 50% of subjects surveyed and was considered a dominant Lactobacillus species of the human gut.
source: In the 1960's and 1970's prior to the emergence of SBO as a major dietary fat source, L. reuteri was recovered from the intestinal tract of 50% of subjects surveyed and was considered a dominant Lactobacillus species of the human gut (Reuter, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Today, L. reuteri is found in less than 10% of humans in the USA and Europe.
source: Today, however, it is found in less than 10% of humans in the USA and Europe (Molin et al., 1993; Qin et al., 2010; Walter et al., 2011), yet it is present at a reported 100% prevalence in rural Papua New Guineans (Martínez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: L. reuteri is present at a reported 100% prevalence in rural Papua New Guineans.
source: Today, however, it is found in less than 10% of humans in the USA and Europe (Molin et al., 1993; Qin et al., 2010; Walter et al., 2011), yet it is present at a reported 100% prevalence in rural Papua New Guineans (Martínez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Human L. reuteri strains show very little genetic variation.
source: Moreover, human L. reuteri strains show very little genetic variation (Duar et al., 2017; Oh et al., 2010), and one human associated lineage of L. reuteri appears to have arisen approximately when SBO consumption increased (Walter et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: One human associated lineage of L. reuteri appears to have arisen approximately when SBO consumption increased.
source: Moreover, human L. reuteri strains show very little genetic variation (Duar et al., 2017; Oh et al., 2010), and one human associated lineage of L. reuteri appears to have arisen approximately when SBO consumption increased (Walter et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In humans, L. reuteri forms neither high gastric populations nor biofilms.
source: In humans, L. reuteri forms neither high gastric populations nor biofilms (Frese et al., 2011; Walter, 2008), thus human-derived L. reuteri strains may have survived increased exposure to 18:2 by developing resistance.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Human-derived L. reuteri strains may have survived increased exposure to 18:2 by developing resistance.
source: In humans, L. reuteri forms neither high gastric populations nor biofilms (Frese et al., 2011; Walter, 2008), thus human-derived L. reuteri strains may have survived increased exposure to 18:2 by developing resistance.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the lack of biofilm formation in humans.

claim: Some human L. reuteri strains are resistant to 18:2, but not all.
source: Indeed, we did observe that some human L. reuteri strains are resistant to 18:2, but not all.
evidence: This is a primary finding from testing human L. reuteri strains.

claim: The increase in SBO consumption may have conspired with other facets of modernization to reduce the prevalence of L. reuteri in Western populations.
source: While the increase in SBO consumption may have conspired with other facets of modernization to reduce the prevalence of L. reuteri in Western populations, it did not appear to have resulted in a selective sweep of 18:2 resistant L. reuteri.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the decline of L. reuteri in Western populations.

claim: The increase in SBO consumption did not appear to have resulted in a selective sweep of 18:2 resistant L. reuteri.
source: While the increase in SBO consumption may have conspired with other facets of modernization to reduce the prevalence of L. reuteri in Western populations, it did not appear to have resulted in a selective sweep of 18:2 resistant L. reuteri.
evidence: This is an inference based on the variation in 18:2 resistance among human L. reuteri strains.

claim: Dietary components have the potential to inhibit microbes directly through their toxicity.
source: Dietary components have the potential to inhibit microbes directly through their toxicity, or indirectly by promoting the growth of other, more fit, microbes.
evidence: This is a general statement about mechanisms by which diet can affect microbes.

claim: Dietary components have the potential to inhibit microbes indirectly by promoting the growth of other, more fit, microbes.
source: Dietary components have the potential to inhibit microbes directly through their toxicity, or indirectly by promoting the growth of other, more fit, microbes.
evidence: This is a general statement about mechanisms by which diet can affect microbes.

claim: Fatty acids are generally toxic to many lactobacilli.
source: While FAs are generally toxic to many lactobacilli, this work suggests that toxicity is greatly reduced when lactobacilli are host-associated.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the manuscript and previous literature.

claim: Toxicity of fatty acids to lactobacilli is greatly reduced when lactobacilli are host-associated.
source: While FAs are generally toxic to many lactobacilli, this work suggests that toxicity is greatly reduced when lactobacilli are host-associated.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations in the manuscript.

claim: The effect of 18:2 on the microbial community was evident from analysis of the live cells but not for the total cell population.
source: The effect of 18:2 on the microbial community was evident from analysis of the live cells but not for the total cell population: microbiomes within a diet-group could be distinguished by gavage treatment only when the live-only aliquot was analyzed (live-only; weighted UniFrac, n = 23 for LF diet: adonis, pseudo-F = 4.78, 15% of variance explained, p = 0.022; n = 21 for HF diet: adonis, pseudo-F = 7.84; 28% of variance explained, p = 0.003; also see Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from 16S rRNA gene sequencing, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Microbiomes within a diet-group could be distinguished by gavage treatment only when the live-only aliquot was analyzed (live-only; weighted UniFrac, n = 23 for LF diet: adonis, pseudo-F = 4.78, 15% of variance explained, p = 0.022; n = 21 for HF diet: adonis, pseudo-F = 7.84; 28% of variance explained, p = 0.003).
source: The effect of 18:2 on the microbial community was evident from analysis of the live cells but not for the total cell population: microbiomes within a diet-group could be distinguished by gavage treatment only when the live-only aliquot was analyzed (live-only; weighted UniFrac, n = 23 for LF diet: adonis, pseudo-F = 4.78, 15% of variance explained, p = 0.022; n = 21 for HF diet: adonis, pseudo-F = 7.84; 28% of variance explained, p = 0.003; also see Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from 16S rRNA gene sequencing, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: 18:2 compromised select microbes, thereby decreasing their abundances and altering the abundances of other live microbes.
source: This observation suggests that 18:2 compromised select microbes, thereby decreasing their abundances and altering the abundances of other live microbes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differences between live-only and total microbiomes after 18:2 gavage.

claim: For both diets, although the jejunal contents from saline-gavaged mice showed differences in the live-only and total diversity, this difference was greater in mice gavaged with 18:2 (p < 0.01 for LF diet, p < 10−7 for HF diet, Kruskal-Wallis tests).
source: Indeed, we observed that for both diets, although the jejunal contents from saline-gavaged mice showed differences in the live-only and total diversity, this difference was greater in mice gavaged with 18:2 (p < 0.01 for LF diet, p < 10−7 for HF diet, Kruskal-Wallis tests) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from 16S rRNA gene sequencing, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: While compromised cells exist in the saline control animals, 18:2 caused additional cells to be compromised.
source: Hence, while compromised cells exist in the saline control animals, 18:2 caused additional cells to be compromised.
evidence: This is an inference based on the greater difference between live-only and total diversity in 18:2 gavaged mice.

claim: The difference in beta-diversity distance between live-only and total aliquots was greater for the HF than the LF diet samples, suggesting that the HF-diet conditioned microbiome was disrupted to a greater extent by 18:2 than the LF-diet microbiome.
source: We note that this difference (beta-diversity distance) was greater for the HF than the LF diet samples (Figure 4B), suggesting that the HF-diet conditioned microbiome was disrupted to a greater extent by 18:2 than the LF-diet microbiome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of beta-diversity distances between diets, shown in Figure 4B.
